title: The girl who made a village's story heard
shortDescription: A Yazidi girl from a farming village in northern Iraq who survived three months of enslavement by ISIS after her mother and six brothers were killed — she escaped, told the world her story, and won the Nobel Peace Prize for ending sexual violence in war.
introduction: Nadia Murad was born in 1993 in Kocho, a small Yazidi farming village at the foot of the Sinjar Mountains in northern Iraq — the youngest of eleven children, raised among olive trees and a faith the rest of the region did not share. On 3 August 2014, the fighters of ISIS surrounded her village, killed the men, took the older women to the mountains to die, and carried the young women and girls into slavery. Nadia's mother and six of her brothers were killed that day. Nadia herself was sold from captor to captor for months before she escaped. She did what almost no survivor of such a trauma has ever done: she told the whole world, refused to be silenced, and won the Nobel Peace Prize. This is her story.

chapters.heading: A village under the mountain
paragraphs: Kocho sits on the green belt of the Sinjar plain, a cluster of stone houses and farms that rise toward the mountain that gives the region its name. Its people were Yazidis: a Kurdish-speaking religious minority whose faith — a blend of ancient and Abrahamic traditions centered on a supreme God and his angels — made them outsiders in the Muslim-majority regions around them. They were farmers, shepherds, traders; their town was small and quiet. Nadia Murad, born there in 1993, was the youngest of eleven children of a farming family, and her early memory of the village is one of near-idyllic order: school, chores, the work of the land, and the unshakeable knowledge of who she was and where she belonged.

The Yazidis had long lived under suspicion. For centuries they had been labelled 'devil worshippers' by outsiders who did not understand them, and they had survived more than seventy documented attempts at their destruction over their history. In 2014 the storm finally arrived, in the form of a new and merciless enemy. The self-styled Islamic State, fresh from a sweep across Iraq and Syria, took Mosul in June of that year. It then turned west toward the Sinjar region, whose Yazidi population it had already marked, in its own propaganda, for annihilation. The villagers knew war was coming; they could not have conceived of what the war would do to them.

Nadia's family hoped to leave. As ISIS advanced through the region in the summer of 2014, many Yazidi families — hers among them — packed what they could and began to move out of Kocho. Then a new order arrived, from the fighters and from the tribal leaders who came to negotiate: the villagers would not be permitted to leave. They were told they would be protected, that they were neighbours, that there was nothing to fear. On the morning of 3 August 2014, the full catastrophe broke over the village. Their neighbours were not protected. They were encircled.

chapters.heading: August 3, 2014
paragraphs: In the small hours of 3 August 2014, ISIS fighters sealed off the roads around Kocho. Over the following days a terrible, methodical routine was carried out across the Sinjar area in what the United Nations would later call genocide. The men and older boys of the village were separated from the women and marched away; most would be shot or left to die. The younger women and girls were rounded up for a different fate. According to the accounts of survivors, the killers took Nadia's mother and six of her brothers; her mother was shot, and two of her brothers were also killed before her eyes. The rest of her family — her other siblings and her nephews — were taken away, and she did not see them alive again.

Nadia was among the women and girls herded onto trucks and driven away. She was nineteen. Across the whole of Sinjar, the numbers were staggering: an estimated five thousand Yazidi civilians killed in a matter of days, and some seven thousand women and girls abducted and sold into slavery. Nadia was taken first to an ISIS stronghold, where she would spend the next months being passed from one armed man to another — sold, bartered, and enslaved. She was beaten when she resisted, and she saw other girls, some younger than thirteen, forced into the same captivity. The testimonies she would later give to the world's courts and parliaments were, by her own account, only a fraction of what she endured.

The horror had a purpose. ISIS did not merely loot and rape; it declared its sexual slavery a religious right, ran the trade as a bureaucracy, and sold Yazidi girls in markets where they were priced like livestock. The enslavement was aimed at destroying the Yazidi people at their root — by murdering the men who could father them, and by breeding out their faith through the forced bearing of the captors' children. Nadia understood this even as she lived it, and it was the knowledge that she was a pawn in an ethnic-cleansing machine, not merely a victim of one man's cruelty, that hardened her resolve to survive and to bear witness. Her first act of resistance was simply not to die.

media.caption: Sinjar in 2014 — the mountain whose refuge saved hundreds of thousands of Yazidis, and whose plain was drenched in their blood.

chapters.heading: The months of silent endurance
paragraphs: Nadia was enslaved for about three months, though the time would distort itself into something heaving and endless. She was held in several towns, moved between houses and compounds belonging to ISIS commanders, and passed among captors who treated her, in her own later words, as a piece of property to be consumed and discarded. She was given a new name, forced to convert, and threatened, along with the other Yazidi girls in her captivity, that she would be killed if she tried to flee. When she did attempt to escape, the beating that followed was severe enough to hospitalize her. She has said that one of the hardest things she had to do was simply keep living, long past the point where survival felt possible.

Her testimony is one of the most sustained attempts at documentation of this particular crime: not only in the memoir she would later write, but in the statistics and patterns she reported to investigators — the auctions, the 'marriages,' the prices, the medical torture, the children of rape that ISIS planned to raise as Muslims, the orders to forget her own language and faith. United Nations investigators and human-rights lawyers would later describe her evidence as among the most important gathered on ISIS's crimes, precisely because she had refused to keep silent about what was done to her. She was twenty-one years old, and she was converting her private suffering into public documentation.

It is almost impossible to describe the interior of those months, and Nadia has never pretended to describe them fully. What she has emphasized instead is what kept her from collapse: the other girls around her, her sisters' faces in her mind, and a sheer animal refusal to give ISIS the final victory. She has spoken often of deliberately memorizing as much as she could — names, faces, locations, markets — the way a prisoner of war files intelligence for a future court. She did not know, during those months, whether she would live to speak. She behaved as though she might.

And then an unlooked-for door opened. After the beating that followed her failed escape, when the house's captor had to step out, she slipped away through an unlocked door and began to run. It would take weeks, seasons of fear, and the kindness of strangers — including a Muslim family who hid her, and smugglers who moved her toward safety — before she reached the refugee camp in the Kurdish region of Iraq where the nightmare finally ended.

chapters.heading: The escape, and the telling
paragraphs: Nadia escaped her captors in the autumn of 2014 and made her way to a refugee camp in Dohuk, in the Kurdish region of northern Iraq. She was lucky, and she knew it: several of her family members had been killed, some of her sisters were still captive or missing, and the Yazidi community around her was a landscape of graves. Even in the camps there was no safety from memory. She spent her first months of freedom doing what every survivor does: looking for her family. Some were found alive; many were not. The geography of her life had been changed forever, and no camp could give it back.

The turning point came when she decided to speak. In December 2015, barely a year after her escape, she addressed the United Nations Security Council in New York — the first survivor of ISIS's sexual slavery to testify to that body — telling the ambassadors plainly: 'ISIS came to my village and killed the men who could have protected us... They did not want us to live; they did not want us to remember our names.' She asked the world to recognize the Yazidi genocide and to bring the survivors home. The address, and the flood of coverage that followed it, made her a public figure almost overnight: the girl with a calm face and a terrible quiet voice who insisted the world stop pretending it could not hear.

She was sponsored, mentored, and brought before Parliament in Britain and the European Union; she worked for a time with a foundation in Germany, where she settled as a refugee; and in September 2016 the United Nations appointed her Goodwill Ambassador for the Dignity of Survivors of Human Trafficking — the first time that title had been given to a person who had actually lived through the crime it described. She had been sold at nineteen as a nameless thing. At twenty-three she stood before the Security Council and gave herself a name everyone would remember. Her next act was to write it all down.

chapters.heading: The Last Girl
paragraphs: In 2017, Hodder & Stoughton published The Last Girl: My Story of Captivity, and My Fight Against the Islamic State, written by Nadia Murad with the journalist Jenna Krajeski. The title referred to something she said quietly, matter-of-factly, to her editors: that if she had not escaped, if the truck had turned left instead of right, she too would have been one of the murdered girls of Kocho — the one who did not get to speak. The memoir was an instant international bestseller and entered the literature of atrocity as one of its most harrowing first-person documents: a nineteen-year-old girl's account of living through a genocide, told without rage and without mercy, in the flat, precise voice of someone who has simply decided that the record must be accurate.

The book became a cultural as well as a legal event. It was translated into dozens of languages, and it was the subject of a documentary, On Her Shoulders (2018), which followed her through the exhausting year in which she became a kind of walking witness — gave the Nobel lecture, endured the interview circuit, and quietly tried to go on breathing while the world asked her, over and over, to relive the worst moments of her life. The German filmmaker who made the documentary said the film was about the cost of her courage: the way a people's entire history of pain had been placed, by the world's need for a face, onto the shoulders of one twenty-four-year-old woman.

The memoir did exactly what she intended it to do. It gave the Yazidi genocide a literary monument, it forced German, British, and American readers to sit with the specific names and places of the Sinjar massacre, and it put a single, irrefutable human face on a crime that statistics had made abstract. It also, in the way of such books, began to heal something she had never asked to carry. She said that writing it was the first time she had allowed herself to believe that telling the story completely — every page, every price — might not destroy her the way her captors had hoped it would. The girl who had been forbidden to remember her name had written her name on the shelf of the world's history books.

chapters.heading: October 2018: the Nobel Peace Prize
paragraphs: On 5 October 2018, the Norwegian Nobel Committee announced that the Peace Prize for that year would be shared by Nadia Murad and the Congolese gynaecologist Denis Mukwege, 'for their efforts to end the use of sexual violence as a weapon of war and armed conflict.' It was the first time the Prize honored the specific crime that defined ISIS's war on the Yazidis — and the first time it had been awarded for a campaign to stop rape being used as a deliberate instrument of policy. For Nadia it was an extraordinary, almost impossible conclusion to a story that had begun, four years earlier, in a slave market. At twenty-five, she was among the youngest people ever to receive the Prize.

In her Nobel lecture in Oslo that December she asked the world for three things: justice, protection, and the right of survivors to be believed. She described the girls sold after her, the ones the world's leaders had not yet found, and she refused the comfortable framing of 'moving on.' 'The world must do for the Yazidis what it did for the victims of the Holocaust and of Rwanda,' she said, 'and that is to recognize their suffering, and to hold the perpetrators to account.' She was not asking for revenge; she was asking for the legal mechanisms that make a genocide repeatable — which is to say, she was asking for the trial and punishment of the men who had done this, and for the survivors to be given back their villages, their dead, and their dignity.

The Prize transformed the mechanics of her advocacy. She used its platform to push the Security Council to investigate ISIS crimes and to bring the women still missing home; she lobbied for a legal definition that would let the survivors of ISIS's sexual violence be recognised as victims; and she donated much of her own money to Yazidi reconstruction. In 2019 she and Mukwege co-founded the Global Survivors Fund, the first organization dedicated specifically to reparations for survivors of conflict-related sexual violence. The woman who had been sold as property had, in the space of five years, become the world's most prominent advocate for the proposition that no war crime is beyond the reach of justice.

chapters.heading: Rebuilding Kocho
paragraphs: The Nobel did not bring back her family, and she has never pretended that it could. Of the eleven children of the Murad household, the 2014 massacre and its aftermath took away her mother and six of her brothers; several of her remaining family members were held captive or displaced. Her village was destroyed, its mosques and shrines reduced to rubble. So Nadia did the only thing a survivor committed to her people can do: she set to work on what remained. In the years after the Prize she scaled up her Nadia's Initiative, a foundation dedicated to rebuilding the Yazidi homeland — repairing the water systems of Sinjar, reconstructing schools and clinics, putting displaced families back into houses that ISIS had emptied, and helping the survivors who returned.

She has approached reconstruction the way she approached testimony: as a form of resistance. The fighters who took Kocho intended not merely to kill Yazidis but to erase them — their villages, their shrines, their uniqueness. Every rebuilt school, every schoolgirl in a Yazidi village with her own name, is a direct answer to that intention. She has also worked relentlessly on the legal front: in 2021, when a German court convicted an ISIS member of genocide and crimes against humanity for crimes including the enslavement of a five-year-old Yazidi girl who had died of thirst the day after the murder of her mother, Nadia welcomed the verdict as the beginning of 'a new era,' proof that the courts of the world could and would catch ISIS's slave-traders wherever their victims' records led.

Her story resolves, at last, into something larger than a single life. She has said that she does what she does because the dead have no voice, and she is alive, so she must be theirs. When she walks today through the rebuilt villages of her people, she is walking in three times at once: the farming childhood that was taken from her, the years of testimony that she endured, and the future of the girls who will grow up with schoolbooks instead of slavery. She is the girl who refused to be the last girl — and the world, finally, heard her.

This is the real weight of her Nobel: not that one woman's suffering was honored, but that a people's suffering was recognized as a crime against humanity. Genocide commemorations around the world now name Sinjar and Kocho alongside Srebrenica and Rwanda, and that — the schoolgirl's story told until the world had to listen — is the victory her enemies never imagined.
